title: Patterns of settlement in the English countryside

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For such a small country, England shows a remarkable variety of patterns of human settlement. We tend to think of the countryside as containing numerous villages of a standard layout, but it is vastly more complicated than this. There are wide areas where the village is a rarity, where instead the church stands alone, with perhaps an inn or a school beside it to mark some sort of centre, but the administrative district itself, the parish, also shows a scattering of farmsteads standing alone on their hillsides or in their valleys, and here and there farmhouses in pairs, or in a small group of three or four clustered together to form a hamlet.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The village is more characteristic of the drier, arable, lowland east of England, while the hamlet and single farmstead are more common on the wetter, hillier and pastoral western side, although both patterns can be found to some degree in all parts of the country.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: These differences date back many centuries – perhaps even more than two thousand years. The explanation relates to the major differences of farming. In predominantly arable country, such as the east – that is, areas where crops were grown – families tended to live together in villages because of a basic shortage of capital equipment, above all the eight oxen which made up each plough-team. Few families possessed their own unit, and several households contributed the oxen to make up a single team. Again, arable farming under the open-field system which prevailed in Europe for many centuries required co-operation at every season of the farming year, a co-operation secured in most places by scores of by-laws which all had to obey. And more than that, the clearance of new land for farming, from the surrounding woods, heaths and marshes, also required co-operation, not only of one village, but often of several villages working together. This was also the case in watery areas requiring the construction of dikes. The upkeep of these dikes demanded the same co-operation over the succeeding centuries.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: On the other hand, as one moves westwards the village becomes rarer because the farming is mainly pastoral, focused usually on sheep or cows. No capital equipment was needed, not even special buildings at first, for people, sheep and cows lived under the same roof in ‘long houses’, an ancient type which can still be seen on and around the south-western moorlands. No need to co-operate, no community rules. The pastoral farmer was his own boss and could live where he liked, provided he had water and shelter. So we get the isolated farmstead, probably from Iron Age times onwards.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The hamlet, where only perhaps three or four farmsteads were grouped together, is harder to account for. It could have been started by the division of a given piece of land between two or three sons living near the ancestral homestead, or it may have been settled by a small group right at the start. Yet it never grew beyond a certain point, never became a village with its own church and later on its own small shops. It remained a distinctive type of human settlement, particularly in Wales.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The village, on the other hand, was settled in one go by a small group of families. They looked first of all for an unfailing water supply. The most obvious source would be a stream, but there were also springs, ponds and wells. For the majority of villages a dry, usually gravelly, soil was the next requirement. Most villages also looked for a sheltered site and many lie in gentle hollows that cut off the worst of the weather. However, some upland sites, apparently open to every wind that blows, show evidence of long prehistoric and later occupation.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The village is, we now know, a very complex form of settlement. The oldest maps we have of village shapes date from the late sixteenth century when the art of surveying (for big landowners) had developed, giving us a graphic picture of the landscape four hundred years ago. Yet it is clear that we cannot jump to conclusions about the original shape and size of a village from even the earliest maps. Archaeology has shown that villages have long been in a continual state of flux. The original church could be moved to a new site for the sake of some large-scale rearrangement. New streets could be formed, a whole village shape altered.

content: For many centuries, England has been divided into small administrative units called parishes. While many contain a village, some parishes consist only of a church, together with some isolated {{20}}, sometimes grouped in a hamlet.

Villages were more commonly established in districts where the practice of {{21}} farming made co-operation a necessity. One form of co-operation was to carry out ploughing with a team of eight oxen belonging to different families. Whole villages co-operated to carry out the {{22}} of woodland, and to build {{23}} where water was a threat.
In areas where {{24}} farming was more common, farmers and animals were generally housed together in isolated dwellings called {{25}}.
Hamlets may have been created through the {{26}} of land among a farmer’s descendants, or established by a small group of people.
